CALL.meaning: Incoming remote call recorded by the receiving component; its elapsed interval includes work delegated to other components.
CALL.read: Use Context and Func to locate BSL, and CallID with client identities to find the caller. duration and CpuTime are microseconds; Memory/MemoryPeak and disk InBytes/OutBytes are bytes. Nested SDBL/DB events can explain part of this interval.
CALL.badSigns: A call exceeds the operation's measured budget, repeats per processed row, or has a MemoryPeak that grows with the result set.
CALL.traps: One CALL is not necessarily one user action. Summing nested calls or adding their DB durations double counts elapsed work.
CALL.fixes: Use the scenario profile to separate SQL, waits and exchanges; batch repeated server work and reduce form data when that component dominates.
CALL.cost: Unfiltered CALL records scale with remote-call frequency; Context adds stack text to each record.

SCALL.meaning: Outgoing remote call recorded by the component making the call.
SCALL.read: Match CallID, ClientID/DstClientID and IName/MName to a receiving CALL within compatible intervals. duration is microseconds; inspect the receiver's nested work before attributing the delay.
SCALL.badSigns: Repeated calls to the same MName during one action, or a long SCALL whose receiver also runs slowly.
SCALL.traps: Starkov's pairing method needs both sides. [unverified] Subtracting CALL from SCALL does not isolate pure network time without validating the pair and its boundaries.
SCALL.fixes: Combine per-row requests into one server call; investigate the receiving CALL and measure exchange time separately.
SCALL.cost: Busy clients can emit many short SCALL records; duration filtering hides call-count problems.

SDBL.meaning: Operation against the platform data model, including queries and transaction actions.
SDBL.read: Read Func, Sdbl, Context and t:connectID. BeginTransaction, CommitTransaction and RollbackTransaction delimit transactions; inspect nested DB events for the physical SQL. Record duration is microseconds.
SDBL.badSigns: Repeated Sdbl text in a loop, or long transaction intervals with TLOCK waiters; large SDBL intervals unexplained by captured DB work need further profiling.
SDBL.traps: HoldConnection and transaction markers are not SQL statements. Adding SDBL duration to nested DB duration counts the same work twice.
SDBL.fixes: Replace repeated model queries with a batch; move permissible computation outside transactions and inspect the corresponding DB plan.
SDBL.cost: SDBL includes frequent data-model operations and transaction markers; all-properties capture can produce large volumes.

DBMSSQL.meaning: Execution of a SQL statement by Microsoft SQL Server on behalf of 1C.
DBMSSQL.read: Read Sql and parameters with Context; dbpid identifies the DBMS connection. Compare duration in microseconds, returned Rows and RowsAffected. Optional planSQLText explains access; lka/lkp annotate observed blocking.
DBMSSQL.badSigns: A SQL fingerprint dominates cumulative elapsed time, or a slow statement has confirmed blocking or excessive reads in its plan.
DBMSSQL.traps: Published Infostart examples contain RowsAffected=-1; do not interpret it as negative updates. Physical SQL table names require the investigated infobase's database structure; duration alone does not separate CPU, I/O and waits.
DBMSSQL.fixes: Find the BSL query, inspect actual data, statistics, plan and waits, then adjust predicates, indexes or transaction scope and re-measure.
DBMSSQL.cost: SQL text and parameters make frequent DBMSSQL records large; plans and DBMS lock polling add instrumentation cost even when output is filtered.

DBPOSTGRS.meaning: Execution of SQL by PostgreSQL on behalf of the platform.
DBPOSTGRS.read: Use Sql, Context and dbpid to locate the BSL operation and DBMS connection. duration is microseconds. With optional planSQLText, compare estimated and actual rows and account for loops; actual time is milliseconds.
DBPOSTGRS.badSigns: Repeated SQL dominates the operation, actual row counts diverge from estimates, or a measured plan spends most time scanning or joining excess data.
DBPOSTGRS.traps: PostgreSQL cost is an estimate in planner units, not seconds. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes SQL; platform connection settings affect reproducibility.
DBPOSTGRS.fixes: Check waits and statistics, push selective restrictions into the 1C query, and validate suitable indexes against the measured plan on comparable data.
DBPOSTGRS.cost: DBPOSTGRS can dominate log volume. IBS's five-second example still produced hundreds of MB; use plans on test/development per the official methodology.

DBV8DBENG.meaning: Execution of a statement by the file database engine.
DBV8DBENG.read: Inspect Func, Sql and Context in the process serving the file infobase. duration is microseconds. Optional planSQLText uses file-engine operators such as FULL SCAN, USING INDEX and NESTED LOOP.
DBV8DBENG.badSigns: Repeated long file-engine operations; a FULL SCAN of a large source or nested scans are candidates when measured data volume explains the cost.
DBV8DBENG.traps: A scan operator alone does not prove a defect. File-engine plans have their own notation; SQL Server/PostgreSQL plan rules do not directly apply.
DBV8DBENG.fixes: Restrict the source data in the 1C query, inspect the file-engine plan and compare query/index alternatives over the whole operation.
DBV8DBENG.cost: Capturing every file-engine statement can be voluminous, especially with Sql, Context and plans.

TLOCK.meaning: Managed transactional lock acquisition; elapsed time includes acquisition waits, not the entire time the lock remains held.
TLOCK.read: Read Locks for resource values and modes, Regions for namespaces, and WaitConnections for conflicting t:connectID values. Find each participant's SDBL transaction boundaries; duration is microseconds.
TLOCK.badSigns: WaitConnections is non-empty, especially when unrelated business keys collide or cumulative acquisition time dominates posting.
TLOCK.traps: A short acquisition may hold a resource until a much later commit. Regions alone does not prove a whole-register lock; no WaitConnections is not evidence of a wait.
TLOCK.fixes: Capture all acquisitions and transaction boundaries; narrow lock dimensions, shorten transactions and use a consistent resource order after verifying intersections.
TLOCK.cost: All TLOCK acquisitions can be frequent; keep them during a short locks capture because a duration cutoff can remove the holder.

TTIMEOUT.meaning: The maximum wait for a transactional lock was exceeded.
TTIMEOUT.read: Locate the victim with t:connectID, SessionID and Context; follow WaitConnections into TLOCK and SDBL on all participants. Obtain wait duration from the matching TLOCK, in microseconds.
TTIMEOUT.badSigns: A TTIMEOUT is already a failed lock wait; repeated instances in the same posting context indicate recurring contention.
TTIMEOUT.traps: TTIMEOUT can have zero duration. Its Context identifies the victim, not the transaction that originally acquired the resource.
TTIMEOUT.fixes: Use the locks profile to find the holder; shorten its transaction, reduce the protected resource scope and re-test concurrent posting.
TTIMEOUT.cost: Timeout records are incident-oriented; the acquisition and transaction evidence needed to explain them costs much more than this event alone.

TDEADLOCK.meaning: Detection of a deadlock in managed locking mode.
TDEADLOCK.read: Read DeadlockConnectionIntersections for participant pairs and intersecting resources. Recover their TLOCK acquisitions and SDBL transaction intervals, including short operations.
TDEADLOCK.badSigns: Any TDEADLOCK warrants cycle reconstruction; repeated participant contexts point to a reproducible access-order conflict.
TDEADLOCK.traps: Zero duration does not imply zero impact. This event does not represent every DBMS deadlock; DBMS cycles require the DBMS deadlock report.
TDEADLOCK.fixes: Align resource acquisition order and compatible lock modes in all participating BSL paths; repeat a parallel reproduction and check waits as well as deadlocks.
TDEADLOCK.cost: Deadlock incidents themselves are sparse; full unfiltered participant histories increase capture volume.

EXCP.meaning: Exception reported by the platform, application, network or DBMS; some exceptions accompany abnormal process termination.
EXCP.read: Preserve the entire Descr cause chain, Exception, OSException, Context and DumpFile when present. Use process/session and time to correlate PROC and EXCPCNTX.
EXCP.badSigns: A new recurring Descr, a failed user operation, or EXCP beside an abnormal PROC termination and dump.
EXCP.traps: Multiple components can log the same failure. Normalized Descr groups similar diagnostics but is not an incident count or a substitute for the full original.
EXCP.fixes: Fix the specific BSL/query/permission or environmental error identified by the cause chain; preserve exact platform version and dump for unexplained crashes.
EXCP.cost: Normally relatively small and infrequent according to the platform docs; repeated exceptions and long stacks can create an error storm.

EXCPCNTX.meaning: Snapshot of operations that had started but had not finished when an abnormal condition occurred.
EXCPCNTX.read: SrcName names the original event type. Read the emitted sequence from deepest nesting outward, together with EXCP, process identity and any dump.
EXCPCNTX.badSigns: Unfinished SQL or CALL frames accompanying a crash localize the interrupted operation; inspect the associated exception to classify failure.
EXCPCNTX.traps: These are interrupted-operation snapshots. [unverified] Counting them again as completed SQL/CALL work would distort throughput and duration totals.
EXCPCNTX.fixes: Investigate the deepest unfinished operation with the original exception; retain the stack and dump when escalating a platform failure.
EXCPCNTX.cost: Emission is tied to abnormal conditions rather than every successful call; a deep interrupted stack yields several records.

QERR.meaning: Query compilation or row/field access restriction error; also used for optional external-source NULL validation failures.
QERR.read: Read Descr, platform-language Query and Context under the failing user's permissions. Special NULL validation requires query checkActualNullable=true.
QERR.badSigns: The same Query fails repeatedly, only particular roles fail, or Descr reports a value inconsistent with external-source nullability.
QERR.traps: QERR diagnoses a query error, not a slow query. Enabling checkActualNullable can substantially slow query execution.
QERR.fixes: Correct query syntax or intended access rights; for external data reconcile nullable metadata and actual values rather than hiding the diagnostic.
QERR.cost: Ordinary QERR records follow failures; optional NULL checking adds execution overhead beyond the number of records written.

PROC.meaning: Lifecycle or availability event for an entire platform process, such as start, stop or abnormal termination.
PROC.read: Read process, PID and the lifecycle action/description; correlate the same process with EXCP, EXCPCNTX, ATTN and the configured restart policy.
PROC.badSigns: Explicit abnormal termination, or repeated unexplained worker replacement near failed operations.
PROC.traps: A normal stop/start can be scheduled recycling. Badanov's process-count examples depend on infrastructure and are not universal sizing limits.
PROC.fixes: For a crash preserve the dump and exact build; for excessive recycling compare cluster limits and OS resource measurements before changing settings.
PROC.cost: Platform docs classify PROC as relatively infrequent and small; retaining lifecycle history is cheaper than full SQL capture.

CONN.meaning: Establishment or loss of a client connection to the server.
CONN.read: Read the connection action, client/application, addresses and available identifiers; correlate the interval with SESN and process availability.
CONN.badSigns: Many clients reconnect beside EXCP or abnormal PROC records, rather than a single expected disconnect.
CONN.traps: Client connections, infobase sessions and DBMS connections are separate identities; this is not a log of every SQL connection.
CONN.fixes: Check the failing component and network path, then confirm process health and session restoration using the same reproduction.
CONN.cost: Usually low volume per the platform docs; a reconnection storm increases the number of CONN records.

SESN.meaning: Infobase session lifecycle and assignment of sessions to connections.
SESN.read: Use SessionID and Func with Usr and connection changes to follow the session across CONN events; inspect job history for scheduled work.
SESN.badSigns: [unverified] Repeated restoration or termination of the same workload beside CONN/EXCP is a diagnostic lead, not a standalone failure rule.
SESN.traps: A session can outlive a particular connection. SessionID can be absent when no session is assigned to the thread.
SESN.fixes: Investigate the associated connection loss or exception; compare scheduled-job execution history before changing job scheduling.
SESN.cost: SESN volume follows session creation, termination and reassignment; busy short-session workloads can emit many lifecycle records.

MEM.meaning: Growth in unfreed dynamic memory of a server process between checkpoints when no calls or scheduled jobs are running.
MEM.read: Compare sz/szd in bytes and cn/cnd as fragment counts for the same process. The event's duration spans the two eligible idle checkpoints, not a memory allocation call.
MEM.badSigns: Successive comparable runs leave positive szd/cnd and rising sz/cn; this is a lead for retained-object and dump analysis.
MEM.traps: Not periodic process RSS sampling. No eligible idle checkpoint or no mem generator can explain absent MEM even during memory growth.
MEM.fixes: Use LEAKS creation stacks to narrow retention; compare dumps of the same process before and after growth and inspect object lifetimes.
MEM.cost: The mem generator slows execution, especially parallel workloads; event volume follows observed checkpoint growth rather than a fixed sampling rate.

LEAKS.meaning: Objects retained between configured tracking checkpoints, with their types and creation stacks.
LEAKS.read: Read Descr for repeated object types and creation sites; relate surviving objects to the procedure or server-call checkpoint configured by leaks/point.
LEAKS.badSigns: Objects that are no longer needed accumulate after repeated completion of the same investigated procedure.
LEAKS.traps: A surviving object may still be required by application logic. Coverage is limited to tracked types and checkpoints, not every native allocation.
LEAKS.fixes: Narrow tracking to the implicated procedure; release unnecessary retained references and compare surviving objects after the same workload.
LEAKS.cost: Tracking object creation and checkpoints adds overhead; broad server-call checkpoints and creation stacks can be costly.

ATTN.meaning: Message from the cluster health-monitoring subsystem.
ATTN.read: Read the message type/text, PID and available MemSize, MaxMemSize or MemoryLimits; compare with the affected component's PROC/EXCP and OS monitoring.
ATTN.badSigns: A process is reported unavailable or unresponsive, or memory has reached a configured critical limit.
ATTN.traps: A health warning reports a condition, not necessarily its initial cause; fields depend on the particular message and platform version.
ATTN.fixes: Check the affected process's exceptions and resource use; correct the demonstrated memory or availability constraint before adjusting cluster limits.
ATTN.cost: ATTN follows health notifications rather than every query; repeated critical-state messages can add sustained diagnostic volume.

CLSTR.meaning: Operations that change cluster behavior, including load distribution.
CLSTR.read: Read Event first, then interpret Data for that subtype and platform version; compare performance update metrics and process assignments with OS measurements.
CLSTR.badSigns: Badanov identifies load imbalance and frequent redistribution as reasons to inspect cluster settings and actual resource constraints.
CLSTR.traps: Ordinary cluster changes are not errors. Data does not have one schema for every Event; author sizing examples are not platform thresholds.
CLSTR.fixes: Compare worker assignment and cluster limits with measured CPU/memory pressure; correct the identified placement or capacity constraint.
CLSTR.cost: Volume depends on cluster activity and performance-update messages; wide Data payloads grow with the reported metrics.

SDGC.meaning: Cleanup and compaction of the session-data store.
SDGC.read: Follow InstanceID; compare FilesSize, UsedSize and CopyBytes in bytes by Method=Analyze/Compact. LockDuration is milliseconds, unlike record duration in microseconds.
SDGC.badSigns: UsedSize grows across comparable operations, or LockDuration spikes during the reported pause.
SDGC.traps: This is session-store maintenance, not collection of all BSL heap memory. Large FilesSize alone does not identify the code creating session data.
SDGC.fixes: Locate unnecessary session-data updates; temporarily use sessiondatacontext to obtain origins when needed, then reduce excessive changes.
SDGC.cost: Maintenance records are separate from MEM; sessiondatacontext adds diagnostic execution cost and should be temporary.

VRSREQUEST.meaning: Request to the server for a resource, exposing part of client/server interaction.
VRSREQUEST.read: Read URI, Method, Headers and Body, which is the body size in bytes. Use available vrs-session/sync identifiers to locate the matching response.
VRSREQUEST.badSigns: Many identical requests within one action, or request Body increasing with unnecessary form collections.
VRSREQUEST.traps: Starkov describes VRS correlation; uniform coverage across client modes is [unverified]. VRS intervals do not cover the complete user action.
VRSREQUEST.fixes: Combine unnecessary requests and defer form data that is not needed for opening; measure the action from before form creation.
VRSREQUEST.cost: Request frequency and recorded headers determine volume; all VRS traffic during interactive use can be numerous.

VRSRESPONSE.meaning: Server response to a resource request.
VRSRESPONSE.read: Inspect Status, Phrase, Headers and Body in bytes. Compare a correctly paired request/response interval with the application CALL interval.
VRSRESPONSE.badSigns: An error Status, an oversized response, or a long paired interval when the corresponding BSL work is short.
VRSRESPONSE.traps: [unverified] Transport success such as HTTP 200 does not prove business completion. Pairing by proximity alone can mix concurrent requests.
VRSRESPONSE.fixes: Reduce transferred form attributes/collections and load them on demand; use network and client profiling for remaining transfer or reconstruction time.
VRSRESPONSE.cost: Every resource response can add status/header diagnostics; pair with requests in a bounded scenario capture.

SCRIPTCIRCREFS.meaning: Diagnostic report of circular references between BSL objects.
SCRIPTCIRCREFS.read: Inspect Context and reported object references to locate the assignments that retain the cycle; reproduce the implicated BSL procedure.
SCRIPTCIRCREFS.badSigns: The same object cycle is reported after a procedure should have released its working objects.
SCRIPTCIRCREFS.traps: Detection requires scriptcircrefs and can substantially slow the application; a cycle report does not quantify all process memory growth.
SCRIPTCIRCREFS.fixes: Remove the retaining reference cycle in the identified BSL objects, repeat the reproduction and disable detection afterward.
SCRIPTCIRCREFS.cost: Circular-reference analysis has substantial execution cost and belongs in a focused temporary capture.

LIC.meaning: Licensing lifecycle diagnostics, including license acquisition/release and hardware-identity checks.
LIC.read: Read Func, res when present, and txt/Txt to distinguish initialization, acquisition, release and monitoring. Preserve the exact failure text.
LIC.badSigns: A failed license acquisition or hardware-consistency check coincides with inability to start or continue the intended session.
LIC.traps: Routine successful licensing actions are not faults. Property-name case varies in real JSON; software and hardware license paths differ.
LIC.fixes: Use the exact diagnostic to check available licenses, licensing configuration and hardware identity; verify the same launch can obtain a license.
LIC.cost: LIC follows licensing activity and checks, not SQL throughput; repeated unsuccessful acquisition attempts can enlarge the log.

HASP.meaning: One operation against a hardware protection key.
HASP.read: Decode txt/Txt as operation(inputs)->outputs and inspect its result; correlate LIC and the failing launch to determine user impact.
HASP.badSigns: Repeated hardware-key access errors accompany a failed license acquisition.
HASP.traps: A HASP record alone is not a licensing failure. Operation/result codes require the key vendor's documented meanings; case differs in sample properties.
HASP.fixes: Check hardware-key accessibility and protection software using the reported operation/result, then confirm acquisition through LIC.
HASP.cost: HASP volume follows key accesses; verbose operation diagnostics can repeat during key lookup or licensing retries.

ts.meaning: Completion timestamp in XML date-time notation, for example 2023-08-02T08:48:05.982000.
ts.read: Subtract the record's duration in microseconds to recover its start; compare start/end intervals when finding a parent CALL.
ts.traps: Align recorded clocks/time zones before comparing nodes; completion order is not invocation order.

duration.meaning: Record elapsed duration in microseconds in JSON and modern text logs; 1000000 means one second.
duration.read: Convert to milliseconds by dividing by 1000; use together with ts to place the event in its enclosing interval.
duration.traps: The XML predicate named duration uses 100-microsecond units, unlike record duration. Historical 8.1 text used different units; the exact transition is [unverified].

durationus.meaning: XML duration-filter value in microseconds, not the JSON record's property name; 5000000 selects five seconds.
durationus.read: For manage_tech_log thresholdMs multiply milliseconds by 1000. Use zero/no cutoff when short calls or lock acquisitions must remain visible.
durationus.traps: Filtering on durationus reduces written events; it cannot reconstruct excluded short acquisitions or prove instrumentation is cheap.

Context.meaning: Execution context, generally a multiline BSL stack containing modules, lines and expressions.
Context.read: Follow the stack from the immediate operation back to callers; retain all frames when linking SQL to the BSL query or lock acquisition.
Context.traps: Missing or truncated Context cannot establish a complete caller path; inspect the original record. The context property must be captured.

Descr.meaning: Free-form diagnostic text; exceptions can contain a nested cause chain, while LEAKS includes retained-object descriptions and creation stacks.
Descr.read: For EXCP/QERR read the original cause chain before using a normalized group; for LEAKS compare object types and creation sites across checkpoints.
Descr.traps: One normalized exception description can group several occurrences or component reports; do not replace the original with the fingerprint.

Sql.meaning: Statement text in the physical database engine's SQL dialect, potentially including parameters and physical table names.
Sql.read: Use details to retain the exact SQL/parameters, locate its Context, and compare normalized count/total/max before inspecting a plan.
Sql.traps: Matching normalized SQL does not guarantee identical parameters, data volumes or execution plans.

Query.meaning: Query text associated with a platform query error, in the platform query language rather than physical DBMS SQL.
Query.read: Read beside QERR.Descr and Context to reproduce the error with the same roles and external-source metadata.
Query.traps: Do not send Query text directly to a DBMS as if it were Sql; permissions and platform compilation can fail before SQL execution.

planSQLText.meaning: Database-specific execution-plan text generated when plansql is enabled.
planSQLText.read: Locate expensive scan/join nodes and compare row estimates with measured rows where available. PostgreSQL actual time is milliseconds and rows/time must be interpreted with loops.
planSQLText.traps: Planner cost is not elapsed seconds. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement; the official PostgreSQL methodology limits plan capture to test/development.

Memory.meaning: Bytes allocated and not freed over a server call: a call-level memory change rather than process RSS.
Memory.read: Compare net retention for repeated equivalent CALL contexts; combine with MemoryPeak and same-process checkpoints/dumps to investigate growth.
Memory.traps: A positive net change can be legitimate retained state; this counter alone does not prove a leak.

MemoryPeak.meaning: Peak bytes allocated but not freed during one server call.
MemoryPeak.read: Rank CALL occurrences by peak, then inspect their Context, returned data and report/form workload at comparable sizes.
MemoryPeak.traps: A high temporary peak can be released afterward; distinguish allocation pressure from persistent retention.

CpuTime.meaning: CPU time consumed by CALL in microseconds; documented since platform 8.3.13.
CpuTime.read: Compare CPU and elapsed duration for the same call and its captured children to decide whether to profile computation or investigate waits.
CpuTime.traps: An absent CpuTime is unknown, not zero; do not sum resource counters across nested CALLs as independent work.

InBytes.meaning: Bytes read from disk during a server call, documented with CALL resource counters.
InBytes.read: Compare disk-read changes for the same CALL workload and inspect related queries and storage monitoring.
InBytes.traps: InBytes is disk input, even though some articles interpret it as client/server traffic. Use VRS Body for exchange size.

OutBytes.meaning: Bytes written to disk during a server call.
OutBytes.read: Compare writes for equivalent posting/report operations and correlate with transaction and DB activity before examining storage behavior.
OutBytes.traps: OutBytes is not response-body or network byte count; nested call counters can overlap.

Body.meaning: Size in bytes of the resource request or response body; the value is a size, not the payload text.
Body.read: Compare VRSREQUEST input and VRSRESPONSE output sizes per correctly paired interaction to find excessive form transfer.
Body.traps: CALL InBytes/OutBytes describe a different resource: disk I/O.

process.meaning: Executable/component type such as rphost or 1cv8c, not a numeric PID.
process.read: Identify which component emitted an event before correlating its threads, lifecycle or server/client side of a call.
process.traps: Several processes can have the same process value; retain PID/source directory and time as well.

p:processName.meaning: Server infobase context, often the database name, stored as text.
p:processName.read: Use an exact value to narrow server events to the investigated infobase and verify capture scope before joining sessions.
p:processName.traps: Client or file-mode events may lack this property; an infobase filter can exclude those events.

OSThread.meaning: Operating-system thread identifier represented as a numeric string.
OSThread.read: Within one emitting process and interval, align nested event intervals/depth and identify candidate work on the same thread.
OSThread.traps: [unverified] Equal thread numbers from different nodes/processes or distant time windows do not establish one execution chain.

SessionID.meaning: Infobase session identifier, not a platform or DBMS connection number.
SessionID.read: Follow SESN and CALL activity for the user's session, including changes of connection; narrow time and infobase before requesting chain.
SessionID.traps: May be absent when no session is assigned to a thread; the same session is not a unique call identifier.

t:connectID.meaning: Platform connection identifier used in transactional-lock participant correlation.
t:connectID.read: Follow a TLOCK/TTIMEOUT WaitConnections value to events carrying the matching t:connectID, then inspect their transaction boundaries.
t:connectID.traps: Do not equate its numeric value with SessionID, ClientID or dbpid.

ClientID.meaning: Remote-interaction client identifier, interpreted with the direction and destination of the call.
ClientID.read: Use SCALL ClientID/DstClientID and matching CALL identities with CallID and interface/method to identify candidate endpoints.
ClientID.traps: A numeric match alone does not prove a distributed call pair; node/process and temporal scope still matter.

CallID.meaning: Identifier of a remote call, represented as a numeric string.
CallID.read: Pair compatible SCALL/CALL records using client endpoints, method and interval, then inspect nested work on the receiving side.
CallID.traps: [unverified] Treat uniqueness over an entire multi-node archive as unproven; preserve endpoint and process scope.

dbpid.meaning: Identifier of the DBMS connection executing an operation.
dbpid.read: Map the 1C SQL event to DBMS wait/connection diagnostics; compare lksrc when finding a DBMS blocker.
dbpid.traps: This is a DBMS identity, not t:connectID; capture time and database are needed when investigating reused connections.

Usr.meaning: Infobase user name, a textual attribution rather than a job identifier.
Usr.read: Compare failures under the affected user's roles and data; combine with session, application and job history for scheduled work.
Usr.traps: DefUser alone is not proof of a background job or its business outcome.

Func.meaning: Event-specific operation name, including data-model and lifecycle actions.
Func.read: For SDBL distinguish BeginTransaction, CommitTransaction, RollbackTransaction and HoldConnection from query work; for other events interpret Func in that event's semantics.
Func.traps: Do not count transaction or connection-management functions as executed SQL statements.

Rows.meaning: Number of rows returned by a database operation, recorded as a numeric value.
Rows.read: Compare returned volume to the user's needed result and CALL memory/transfer; inspect the plan separately for actual rows processed at each node.
Rows.traps: Rows is not scanned rows, pages read or an automatic measure of index efficiency.

RowsAffected.meaning: Affected-row count; Infostart's published event examples include the value -1.
RowsAffected.read: Compare known counts with the intended posting/exchange batch size and transaction/lock scope. Treat -1 as unknown for analysis until its meaning for that platform/operation is established.
RowsAffected.traps: Do not interpret -1 as a negative update count or replace it with zero.

Locks.meaning: Managed transactional lock resources, values and modes in the lock acquisition diagnostic.
Locks.read: Compare waiter and candidate holder resources for overlapping values and conflicting modes; inspect the BSL lock construction in Context.
Locks.traps: A namespace match alone does not establish the same protected keys or prove a whole-register lock.

Regions.meaning: Names of managed transactional lock namespaces.
Regions.read: Group contended business resources, then request Locks, Context and transaction intervals to establish their actual extent.
Regions.traps: Regions naming a register does not mean every record of that register was locked.

WaitConnections.meaning: List of platform connections conflicting over managed transactional locks.
WaitConnections.read: Non-empty values identify waiter-side leads: locate matching t:connectID acquisitions and their enclosing transactions across captured processes.
WaitConnections.traps: TLOCK without WaitConnections is not proof of waiting; a reported connection still needs resource/mode and lifetime checks.

DeadlockConnectionIntersections.meaning: Managed deadlock participant pairs and intersections of the locked resources.
DeadlockConnectionIntersections.read: Recover each listed participant's TLOCK acquisitions and transaction interval to reconstruct resource order in both BSL paths.
DeadlockConnectionIntersections.traps: A managed deadlock intersection is not a complete DBMS deadlock graph.

lka.meaning: DBMS blocking-source flag; value 1 means the thread was observed as a source by dbmslocks polling.
lka.read: Find the source's lkaid list, match a victim lkpid and inspect transaction history to locate the resource-acquiring operation.
lka.traps: Annotations attach to a later completed event; its SQL need not be the statement that acquired the lock.

lkp.meaning: DBMS blocking-victim flag; value 1 means the thread was observed waiting.
lkp.read: Read the same record's lkpid and lksrc, then find the source in other working-process logs.
lkp.traps: Observed blocking is not proof of a deadlock cycle; short waits can fall between polls.

lkpid.meaning: Identifier of the DBMS blocking poll attached to a victim, for example 423.
lkpid.read: Join this scalar value to an element of the source lkaid list across worker logs, then check lksrc and context.
lkpid.traps: lkpid is a poll identifier, not an OS PID, SQL statement id or platform connection id.

lkaid.meaning: Comma-separated list of blocking-poll identifiers on a source thread, for example 271,273,274.
lkaid.read: Split the list and find victim records with corresponding lkpid values; retain each participant's DBMS connection and transaction history.
lkaid.traps: The list is populated by dbmslocks observations, polled on DB access no more often than once per two seconds; it is not a continuous trace.

lksrc.meaning: DBMS connection identifier of the blocking source, present on the victim side.
lksrc.read: Use with the victim's lkpid and source's lkaid to identify the holder's dbpid and inspect its earlier transaction operations.
lksrc.traps: Do not resolve lksrc as a platform t:connectID or infer the holder solely from nearby timestamps.

lkpto.meaning: Seconds elapsed since the thread was detected as a DBMS blocking victim.
lkpto.read: Compare with poll linkage and surrounding event times to understand the observed wait history, then inspect the holder transaction.
lkpto.traps: Seconds since detection are neither record microseconds nor a precise timestamp of initial lock acquisition.

lkato.meaning: Seconds elapsed since the thread was detected as a DBMS blocking source.
lkato.read: Follow matching victims and the source's transaction completion to investigate how long the observed source state persists.
lkato.traps: Source-state age begins at detection; it is not the duration of the SQL carrying the annotation.

SrcName.meaning: Original operation's event type on an EXCPCNTX snapshot.
SrcName.read: Interpret each interrupted frame using the referenced event's semantics; read the EXCPCNTX sequence in descending nesting order.
SrcName.traps: SrcName=CALL describes an unfinished operation, not a second completed CALL.

LockDuration.meaning: Session-data store lock duration in milliseconds during garbage-collector work.
LockDuration.read: For a given SDGC InstanceID compare Analyze/Compact lock time with user pauses and changes in UsedSize/FilesSize.
LockDuration.traps: Do not divide this value by 1000 as if it were record duration in microseconds.

sz.meaning: Bytes of dynamic memory occupied by the process at a MEM checkpoint.
sz.read: Compare sz across equivalent idle checkpoints of the same process; combine with szd and retained-object evidence.
sz.traps: This is dynamic memory accounting at eligible checkpoints, not total OS RSS.

szd.meaning: Change in occupied dynamic-memory bytes since the previous MEM event.
szd.read: Follow repeated positive deltas after comparable completed operations and inspect LEAKS stacks or before/after dumps.
szd.traps: A single positive delta can be useful cached state; it does not establish erroneous retention.

cn.meaning: Count of occupied dynamic-memory fragments at a MEM checkpoint.
cn.read: Compare fragment-count growth with sz to distinguish more fragments from a few larger allocations in the same process.
cn.traps: Fragment count is not a count of BSL business objects or active sessions.

cnd.meaning: Change in occupied-fragment count since the previous MEM event.
cnd.read: Use alongside szd to identify repeated fragment accumulation and select comparable checkpoints for retention analysis.
cnd.traps: This delta has count units, not bytes; the interval depends on eligible idle checkpoints.

txt.meaning: Free-form diagnostic text; hardware-key records can encode operation(inputs)->outputs.
txt.read: Read the exact LIC action/result or HASP operation result; retain original spelling and casing when checking vendor documentation.
txt.traps: Real samples use txt, Txt or TXT; property lookup must tolerate case variation without rewriting the original diagnostic.

Sdbl.meaning: Query text in the platform's database-model language, carried by SDBL.
Sdbl.read: Use the SDBL Context to find the BSL origin, then compare its nested physical Sql statements to see how the model operation was translated.
Sdbl.traps: Sdbl, QERR Query and DBMS Sql are different language layers, even when they describe the same business operation.

errors.meaning: Diagnose reported failures and loss of component availability without collecting every successful call or SQL statement.
errors.read: Use for an exception, failed query, disconnect or crash. Read EXCP/QERR first, correlate PROC/CONN/SESN/ATTN, and treat TTIMEOUT/TDEADLOCK as leads requiring participant history; the cutoff is 0 ms.
errors.traps: It does not collect all TLOCK acquisitions or SDBL transaction boundaries, so it cannot identify every holder from an incident alone. Dump generation is separate.
errors.fixes: Repair the exact diagnostic's cause; switch to locks when timeout/deadlock participants are missing.
errors.cost: Normally smaller than SQL capture per platform docs; long exception chains and error/reconnection storms can still be large.

slow-calls.meaning: Find receiving server contexts and outgoing calls that exceed the chosen individual-call cutoff.
slow-calls.read: Use after a slow operation is localized. The default 1000 ms cutoff selects CALL/SCALL; compare count, total/max duration, Context, CpuTime and MemoryPeak, then inspect EXCP for failure.
slow-calls.traps: Short repeated calls are excluded by the default cutoff; nested CALL/SCALL durations overlap, so their totals are not full-user-operation time.
slow-calls.fixes: Use scenario to identify whether SQL, lock waits, computation or form exchange dominates the expensive context, then optimize that component.
slow-calls.cost: Volume falls as the cutoff rises; frequent long calls with full stacks can remain numerous, and filtering hides accumulated short-call cost.

db.meaning: Locate expensive physical SQL and platform data-model operations before a focused plan investigation.
db.read: Use when database work dominates. The default 5000 ms cutoff applies to physical DB events; SDBL and EXCP/QERR remain unfiltered. Inspect Sql/Sdbl, Context and count/total/max. Plans and DBMS lock polling are explicit options.
db.traps: The five-second cutoff is a diagnostic choice, not a platform health limit. Gilev's historical example uses ten seconds; IBS uses five. Official PostgreSQL guidance confines plans to test/development, unlike older article profiles.
db.fixes: Find the BSL query and inspect data, parameters, statistics and waits before changing predicates or indexes; lower the cutoff for repeated short SQL.
db.cost: IBS reports hundreds of MB even above five seconds. SQL/parameters enlarge records; optional plans/polling add overhead beyond output volume.

locks.meaning: Reconstruct managed lock waits, transaction lifetimes and optional observed DBMS blocker relationships.
locks.read: Use during a short concurrent reproduction on all relevant workers. The 0 ms cutoff keeps TLOCK acquisitions, TTIMEOUT/TDEADLOCK, SDBL boundaries and server SQL; optional dbmslocks adds lka/lkp poll linkage.
locks.traps: Filtering short acquisitions loses holders. The bundled event set includes SQL Server/PostgreSQL, not file-engine SQL; add DBV8DBENG when needed. Poll linkage does not prove a DBMS deadlock cycle.
locks.fixes: Check WaitConnections, resource values/modes and transaction lifetime; then shorten scope or align resource order. Obtain a DBMS deadlock report for DBMS cycles.
locks.cost: High acquisition and SQL frequency can produce a large log; bound the reproduction and retain logs from every participant, including short successful holders.

memory.meaning: Separate high call allocation peaks from persistent object retention in one server process.
memory.read: Use after reproducible memory growth. CALL counters localize peaks; mem enables MEM idle-checkpoint counters, and leaks collect=1 with point call=server enables retained-object stacks. The cutoff is 0 ms.
memory.traps: MEM is not periodic RSS; no suitable idle checkpoint can explain absence. LEAKS tracks selected objects and surviving objects can be legitimate; compare the same process/workload.
memory.fixes: Narrow retained-object tracking to the implicated procedure after localization and compare same-process before/after dumps; reduce unnecessary collections or retained references.
memory.cost: mem/leaks instrumentation slows execution, especially parallel workloads; broad checkpoints and creation stacks are more costly than CALL counters alone.

scenario.meaning: Explain one complete reproduced user action across calls, data access, locks and resource exchanges.
scenario.read: Start immediately before one short reproduction and stop immediately after it. At 0 ms, retain CALL/SCALL, VRS request/response, SDBL, database events, managed locks and errors; find the enclosing call and compare child intervals.
scenario.traps: A server-only capture can miss client transfer/reconstruction and other nodes. historyHours=1 is retention, not automatic capture expiry; an unfinished call may not yet have a completion record.
scenario.fixes: Follow details then chain, test the demonstrated query/lock/call/form correction and repeat with the same data, timing boundary and concurrency.
scenario.cost: Potentially the largest bundled profile because it retains short calls and SQL; stop explicitly after the reproduction rather than leaving it as permanent monitoring.

exceptions.meaning: A platform, application or infrastructure exception interrupted or threatened the operation.
exceptions.evidence: EXCP Exception/Descr and Context establish the reported failure; the complete cause chain and user outcome establish impact. Several matching component records do not establish several independent incidents.
exceptions.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for the exception group and read original Descr. 2. Use mode=chain on an occurrence to find surrounding CALL/SQL. 3. Check affected user, exact version and any linked dump.
exceptions.fixes: Correct the evidenced BSL error, access right, query or environment setting; reproduce under the affected user's data and roles.
exceptions.traps: Normalized Descr is an aggregation key. Removing variable text can merge different incidents, so preserve the original chain before choosing a fix.
exceptions.profile: errors collects EXCP and related lifecycle evidence; use scenario when the successful and failed operation paths must be compared.

query-errors.meaning: The platform cannot compile or authorize a query, or detects an external-source nullability mismatch.
query-errors.evidence: QERR Descr, Query and Context identify the failing query and diagnostic; long DB duration without QERR does not prove a compilation or access error.
query-errors.investigate: 1. Read QERR Query/Descr with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to locate the caller and roles. 3. Reproduce the query with the same permissions and external-source metadata.
query-errors.fixes: Repair query syntax or the intended row/field access policy; reconcile external nullability metadata with returned data if that check caused the failure.
query-errors.traps: The optional query checkActualNullable check can slow execution substantially; a missing QERR does not prove every external value was validated.
query-errors.profile: errors includes QERR; db adds the surrounding data-model and physical statements when compilation succeeds far enough to execute SQL.

process-crashes.meaning: A platform process terminated abnormally, losing availability or interrupting work.
process-crashes.evidence: PROC must explicitly describe abnormal termination; correlate EXCP/EXCPCNTX and DumpFile or OS crash evidence. An ordinary process stop/start alone is not a crash.
process-crashes.investigate: 1. Inspect the original PROC action using get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain on nearby exception occurrences for interrupted work. 3. Check exact platform build, restart policy and process dump.
process-crashes.fixes: Fix the demonstrated application/environment cause; preserve the dump and reproduction for platform support when the crash remains unexplained.
process-crashes.traps: Scheduled worker recycling and changed PID are not abnormal-termination proof; distinguish configured replacement from failure.
process-crashes.profile: errors captures PROC, EXCP, EXCPCNTX and ATTN; dump generation is a separate diagnostic setting, not supplied by this capture profile.

lock-timeouts.meaning: A transaction failed because its managed lock wait exceeded the allowed time.
lock-timeouts.evidence: TTIMEOUT establishes the timeout. TLOCK WaitConnections, Locks and matching SDBL transaction boundaries are needed to identify the holder; the victim's Context alone does not identify it.
lock-timeouts.investigate: 1. Read the timeout occurrence with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to follow WaitConnections to candidate holders. 3. Verify intersecting values/modes and their transaction end across all workers.
lock-timeouts.fixes: Shorten the demonstrated holding transaction; move permissible computation out of it and narrow the managed lock to the required keys.
lock-timeouts.traps: TTIMEOUT duration may be zero. Filtering out short successful TLOCK acquisitions can erase the holder even when the long wait remains.
lock-timeouts.profile: locks uses no duration cutoff and captures acquisitions plus transaction boundaries; errors alone detects the timeout but cannot reconstruct its cause.

managed-deadlocks.meaning: Managed transactions acquired conflicting resources in an order that created a deadlock.
managed-deadlocks.evidence: TDEADLOCK DeadlockConnectionIntersections names participant intersections; TLOCK and SDBL history are needed to reconstruct the cycle. A timeout without a cycle is insufficient.
managed-deadlocks.investigate: 1. Read participant intersections in get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain for each captured participant. 3. Reconstruct resource acquisition order and modes through transaction completion.
managed-deadlocks.fixes: Use a consistent register/resource acquisition order in every participating BSL path; choose compatible managed lock modes and shorten transactions.
managed-deadlocks.traps: The detected victim is not the only code path requiring repair. TDEADLOCK is managed-mode evidence, not every DBMS deadlock.
managed-deadlocks.profile: locks collects short TLOCK acquisitions, TDEADLOCK and SDBL boundaries needed for a concurrent reproduction on all relevant nodes.

lock-waits.meaning: A managed lock acquisition waits for another platform connection.
lock-waits.evidence: A TLOCK with non-empty WaitConnections provides waiter evidence; confirm holder identity using t:connectID, intersecting Locks and transaction lifetime. TLOCK without WaitConnections is not a proven wait.
lock-waits.investigate: 1. Inspect wait-bearing TLOCK in get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to find listed connections. 3. Compare Locks values/modes and SDBL transaction intervals before assigning responsibility.
lock-waits.fixes: Reduce conflicting lock scope, shorten the holder's transaction and keep resource order consistent; repeat posting concurrently on distinct business keys.
lock-waits.traps: Regions names a namespace, not the precise protected keys. Acquisition duration is not the entire lock holding interval.
lock-waits.profile: locks retains every acquisition; collect every participant rather than only the waiting user's worker.

dbms-locks.meaning: One DBMS connection blocks another, independently of managed-lock diagnostics.
dbms-locks.evidence: With dbmslocks, lkp=1 identifies an observed victim and lka=1 a source. Join victim lkpid to source lkaid and check lksrc/dbpid. These flags alone do not prove a deadlock cycle.
dbms-locks.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details to retain poll/connection fields. 2. Use mode=chain to locate matching source records across workers. 3. Inspect earlier SQL in the source transaction and DBMS wait diagnostics.
dbms-locks.fixes: Shorten the confirmed blocking transaction, reduce write batches and tune SQL access paths when the plan demonstrates unnecessary locked data.
dbms-locks.traps: Polling occurs on DB access at most once per two seconds. The carrier event can complete after the blocking observation and need not contain the SQL that acquired the resource.
dbms-locks.profile: locks with the explicit dbmslocks option adds poll annotations; collect all working processes and DBMS-side evidence for suspected cycles.

slow-db.meaning: Database work consumes an excessive part of the reproduced operation's elapsed time.
slow-db.evidence: DBMSSQL/DBPOSTGRS/DBV8DBENG duration with Sql and Context establishes expensive statement occurrences. SDBL without statement text is not SQL execution proof; duration alone does not identify CPU, I/O or blocking.
slow-db.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details to inspect original SQL, parameters and counts. 2. Use mode=chain to locate the BSL caller and overlapping waits. 3. Examine the DBMS plan, statistics and actual data volumes.
slow-db.fixes: Apply the proven query correction: selective virtual-table parameters, suitable index keys, fewer repeated queries or shorter transactions; compare the whole operation afterward.
slow-db.traps: A normalized SQL group can contain different parameters/plans. The official PostgreSQL methodology's roughly 50 percent DB share is an investigation lead, not a universal failure boundary.
slow-db.profile: db defaults to a 5000 ms cutoff for individual statements; use scenario or lower the cutoff when many short statements dominate instead.

slow-calls.meaning: A receiving remote call exceeds the response-time budget for the intended user operation.
slow-calls.evidence: CALL duration, Context and resource counters identify expensive contexts; nested DB/TLOCK/SCALL and client timing explain components. Elapsed CALL time alone does not prove slow BSL computation.
slow-calls.investigate: 1. Read representative CALLs with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to inspect nested SQL, waits and outgoing calls. 3. Compare CpuTime, MemoryPeak and full-user-operation timing.
slow-calls.fixes: Optimize the dominant measured component: batch server work, tune the demonstrated query, shorten conflicting transactions or reduce form serialization.
slow-calls.traps: Nested durations overlap. [unverified] Residual time after removing the union of captured child intervals is unexplained time, not automatically BSL CPU.
slow-calls.profile: slow-calls selects calls from 1000 ms by default; scenario retains short children and surrounding work for one bounded reproduction.

memory-peaks.meaning: A server call creates high transient memory demand or leaves memory requiring retention analysis.
memory-peaks.evidence: CALL MemoryPeak ranks peak bytes and Memory shows net change. Repeated MEM sz/szd growth, LEAKS stacks and comparable same-process dumps support retention investigation; one peak or RSS value does not prove a leak.
memory-peaks.investigate: 1. Inspect peak CALL contexts with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to relate report/query result sizes. 3. Compare eligible MEM checkpoints, retained objects and same-process dumps before/after the workload.
memory-peaks.fixes: Reduce unnecessary report/form collections and large intermediate results; release references demonstrated to survive beyond their required lifetime.
memory-peaks.traps: Dump comparisons from different processes or different workloads are not comparable retention evidence; tracked survivors can still be legitimate cached state.
memory-peaks.profile: memory enables mem and leaks checkpoints as well as CALL counters; its instrumentation is intended for focused growth investigations.

many-calls.meaning: One user action makes repeated remote calls whose aggregate cost dominates despite short individual durations.
many-calls.evidence: CALL/SCALL counts by Context and MName within the measured action support the hypothesis; compare counts against processed rows and inspect BSL. A duration-filtered capture cannot establish the full call count.
many-calls.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details to examine repeated contexts/methods. 2. Use mode=chain on representative calls to identify both endpoints. 3. Inspect the BSL loop and compare action sizes.
many-calls.fixes: Combine data and actions into one server call, remove implicit per-row server access and use a context-free server call where form context is unnecessary.
many-calls.traps: [unverified] Call count scaling with rows is a diagnostic hypothesis, not proof of a specific loop until the code is checked.
many-calls.profile: scenario retains short CALL/SCALL; the default slow-calls cutoff would hide the calls needed to establish this pattern.

slow-form.meaning: Opening a managed form is slow across server execution, context transfer and client reconstruction.
slow-form.evidence: Measure from before form opening; CALL/SQL intervals and paired VRS Body/status reveal components. Short SQL/BSL does not rule out large form-context transfer or client work.
slow-form.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for form CALL/SQL and VRS occurrences. 2. Use mode=chain to find corresponding server work. 3. Compare complete opening time and use WPR/WPA or network tools for gaps.
slow-form.fixes: Reduce form attributes and nested collections, load optional data on demand and minimize unnecessary server round trips; re-measure from before opening.
slow-form.traps: Visible row count can be small while hidden form data is large; a timer started inside form code can miss serialization and restoration.
slow-form.profile: scenario captures VRS and calls for a short opening reproduction; obtain client-side logs as well as the server's nodes.

slow-posting.meaning: Document posting is delayed by data queries, transaction work or contention.
slow-posting.evidence: The posting CALL Context, repeated SQL, SDBL transaction markers and wait-bearing TLOCK separate candidates. [unverified] Repetition suggests row-by-row work but requires BSL confirmation.
slow-posting.investigate: 1. Inspect posting SQL and waits with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to relate them to the posting transaction. 3. Compare query count, locked resources and a concurrent reproduction.
slow-posting.fixes: Batch posting queries, pass applicable virtual-table filters, shorten the transaction and narrow locks while preserving register movement and posting correctness.
slow-posting.traps: Posting concurrency and data volume change the outcome; a faster isolated run does not prove the contention defect is fixed.
slow-posting.profile: scenario captures the posting call and SQL together; locks provides full participant history when contention is the dominant branch.

background-jobs.meaning: A background or scheduled job runs slowly, fails or does not produce its expected business result.
background-jobs.evidence: CALL Func/Module/Meth and JobScheduler application identify job work; SQL/errors and actual job history establish execution/outcome. DefUser or an absent completed CALL alone does not prove job launch state.
background-jobs.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for the job's methods and errors. 2. Use mode=chain to inspect SQL/waits in that execution. 3. Compare launch/completion history, schedule and business outputs.
background-jobs.fixes: Avoid conflicting schedules, reduce unnecessary parallel work and optimize the demonstrated query or loop in the job's BSL procedure.
background-jobs.traps: An active unfinished call may not yet be logged; technical completion does not prove the business operation produced the intended result.
background-jobs.profile: scenario is the bundled starting point for a bounded job execution; errors captures failure history when continuous SQL detail is unnecessary.

index-scan.meaning: A query's access path reads substantially more data than the operation needs.
index-scan.evidence: Expensive DB Sql/Context plus a measured plan, selectivity and data volume support an index mismatch. An operator name or low returned Rows alone does not prove excess reads.
index-scan.investigate: 1. Read SQL/parameters with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to locate the BSL query. 3. Compare estimated versus actual rows, access conditions and candidate index key order.
index-scan.fixes: Align index keys with selective predicates and joins, or rewrite the specific 1C query condition; verify plan and total operation cost after the change.
index-scan.traps: An index suggestion needs the actual query/data/plan; creating indexes automatically from a slow duration can add write cost without fixing the cause.
index-scan.profile: db localizes expensive SQL; request plans separately on test/development and preserve parameters for comparable execution.

seq-scan-not-proof.meaning: A sequential scan has been mistaken for sufficient proof of a query defect.
seq-scan-not-proof.evidence: DBPOSTGRS planSQLText may show Seq Scan, but table size, selected fraction and actual work determine whether it is expensive. The presence of Seq Scan alone proves only the chosen access method.
seq-scan-not-proof.investigate: 1. Inspect the plan and SQL in get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to find the operation's contribution. 3. Compare actual rows, loops and measured alternatives on representative data.
seq-scan-not-proof.fixes: Keep an efficient scan when it serves the data volume; change predicates/indexes only after a measured alternative improves the whole operation.
seq-scan-not-proof.traps: PostgreSQL cost is not seconds; an estimated plan without actual execution cannot establish measured time or returned rows.
seq-scan-not-proof.profile: db with optional test/development plans supplies the access-path candidate; a small-table scan can remain healthy despite appearing in the capture.

temp-table-index.meaning: Repeated access to a temporary result lacks a useful access path for the batch's joins or lookups.
temp-table-index.evidence: Repeated temporary-table SQL and an expensive plan join/lookup support this candidate; confirm the originating BSL query batch and used keys. A temporary table name by itself proves no inefficiency.
temp-table-index.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details to preserve the complete SQL batch and parameters. 2. Use mode=chain to locate its query context. 3. Check reuse and measure creation, indexing and consumption together.
temp-table-index.fixes: Materialize the necessary intermediate result and use the 1C query INDEX BY clause for the keys actually reused; compare whole-batch cost including index creation.
temp-table-index.traps: Normalized temporary-table renumbering is only a grouping aid. An index can cost more to build than it saves for a small or single-use result.
temp-table-index.profile: db collects batch statements; lower its cutoff or use scenario so short table/index creation costs remain in the comparison.

virtual-table-filter.meaning: A query processes too much virtual-table data before applying useful restrictions.
virtual-table-filter.evidence: SQL/Context leading to a BSL virtual-table query with applicable restrictions outside its parameters supports the candidate; verify its plan and semantics. Long duration alone does not identify this construction.
virtual-table-filter.investigate: 1. Inspect physical SQL and Context in get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to locate the originating query. 3. Compare virtual-table parameters and outer predicates on representative balances/turnovers.
virtual-table-filter.fixes: Pass applicable restrictions into the virtual-table parameters in the 1C query and verify identical business results, including periods and dimensions.
virtual-table-filter.traps: Moving a condition can change balance/turnover semantics; optimize only restrictions valid for that virtual table's parameter contract.
virtual-table-filter.profile: db finds expensive virtual-table expansions; include SDBL Context and obtain the original BSL query to validate parameter placement.

subquery-joins.meaning: A join to a complex subquery or virtual table produces an expensive expanded database plan.
subquery-joins.evidence: DB Sql/Context and the BSL query identify the construction; measured plan rows/loops establish cost. The mere presence of a subquery is not proof it needs materialization.
subquery-joins.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for SQL and available plan. 2. Use mode=chain to identify the full query batch. 3. Compare join estimates and intermediate result sizes.
subquery-joins.fixes: Materialize suitable intermediate data in temporary tables, index the reused keys and compare total batch execution with equivalent results.
subquery-joins.traps: Splitting a query adds materialization work; evaluating only the final SELECT hides temporary-result creation costs.
subquery-joins.profile: db localizes costly joins; use a sufficiently low cutoff to retain every phase of a candidate temporary-table rewrite.

query-predicates.meaning: A query predicate causes avoidable expansion or prevents an efficient selective access path.
query-predicates.evidence: Expanded SQL/Context and a measured plan must lead to a specific OR condition, computation or composite-reference dereference in the BSL query. A complex-looking expression alone is insufficient.
query-predicates.investigate: 1. Read original SQL/parameters with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to locate the BSL predicate. 3. Compare its types, selectivity and plan against a semantically equivalent rewrite.
query-predicates.fixes: Rewrite the demonstrated condition, constrain composite references to the required type and simplify index-blocking calculations where equivalent; check result and plan.
query-predicates.traps: Do not mechanically split every OR or add every possible reference type; preserve NULL, type and duplicate-result semantics.
query-predicates.profile: db captures the expanded SQL; keep Context and inspect the source query because physical SQL alone obscures platform reference semantics.

n-plus-one-sql.meaning: A BSL operation issues a database query repeatedly for individual items instead of retrieving a suitable set.
n-plus-one-sql.evidence: [unverified] Repeated normalized Sql within one CALL, with count growing as processed rows grow, is a candidate. Confirm the loop in BSL; unrelated calls sharing a fingerprint are insufficient.
n-plus-one-sql.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details to inspect SQL count and original parameters. 2. Use mode=chain to place repetitions inside one call. 3. Inspect the Context's BSL loop and compare two input sizes.
n-plus-one-sql.fixes: Replace the query inside the loop with a batch/set query over the needed keys, then process the resulting selection or indexed temporary result.
n-plus-one-sql.traps: Literal normalization can merge distinct per-item statements; repetition establishes frequency, not redundant work or an automatic right to cache results.
n-plus-one-sql.profile: scenario or db with thresholdMs=0 retains the short statements; the default five-second db cutoff can hide the whole pattern.

long-transaction.meaning: A transaction holds resources while performing work that prolongs contention.
long-transaction.evidence: SDBL BeginTransaction through CommitTransaction/RollbackTransaction establishes an interval; matched TLOCK/DBMS victims demonstrate impact. A long CALL alone is not a transaction boundary.
long-transaction.investigate: 1. Inspect transaction Func markers using get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to follow the connection through SQL and lock acquisition. 3. Check waiters before commit and identify movable computation.
long-transaction.fixes: Move permissible calculations and external work outside the transaction, reduce batch size and keep the protected read/write sequence as short as correctness permits.
long-transaction.traps: Short SQL does not imply short lock holding. Missing begin/end markers or filtered history prevents a complete holding-time conclusion.
long-transaction.profile: locks keeps SDBL boundaries and acquisitions without a duration cutoff; collect the holder even when it belongs to another worker.

wide-managed-lock.meaning: A managed lock protects a wider business-key range than the operation requires.
wide-managed-lock.evidence: TLOCK Locks must show broad values/modes and unrelated keys must conflict; verify BSL lock construction and transaction lifetime. Regions containing a register name is insufficient.
wide-managed-lock.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details to read complete Locks and Context. 2. Use mode=chain for waiter and candidate holder. 3. Compare requested lock dimensions with the actual business keys.
wide-managed-lock.fixes: Specify the required register dimensions/values in managed locks and shorten their transaction lifetime; validate concurrent operations on different keys.
wide-managed-lock.traps: [unverified] A whole-register-lock diagnosis remains a hypothesis until resource coverage and the code setting it are confirmed.
wide-managed-lock.profile: locks captures resource values and short acquisitions; preserve Context and all participant processes to test the scope hypothesis.

lock-escalation.meaning: SQL Server converts many fine-grained locks into a broader lock that blocks other work.
lock-escalation.evidence: TJ SQL/connection evidence localizes the candidate; Microsoft requires lock_escalation Extended Events and a blocking table S/X lock to confirm it. A table lock or TJ lka flag alone is insufficient.
lock-escalation.investigate: 1. Inspect affected SQL with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to link the transaction and victims. 3. Correlate SQL Server lock_escalation events and the blocking lock mode/resource.
lock-escalation.fixes: Use shorter transactions, smaller modification batches and efficient selective queries; preserve posting/exchange correctness while reducing locked data.
lock-escalation.traps: Do not disable lock escalation as an automatic first fix. A table lock can arise for reasons other than escalation.
lock-escalation.profile: locks with dbmslocks links observed DBMS participants; collect SQL Server Extended Events separately for escalation proof.

dbms-deadlock.meaning: Database transactions formed a deadlock cycle detected by the DBMS.
dbms-deadlock.evidence: EXCP with a DBMS deadlock diagnostic plus SQL Server xml_deadlock_report or PostgreSQL deadlock log establishes the DBMS cycle. lka/lkp identifies blocking but cannot prove a cycle.
dbms-deadlock.investigate: 1. Read the DBMS exception and SQL in get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to locate participant contexts. 3. Read the DBMS graph/log to reconstruct resources and access order.
dbms-deadlock.fixes: Change the participating BSL/SQL paths to acquire resources in a consistent order; shorten transactions and validate under concurrent load.
dbms-deadlock.traps: TDEADLOCK concerns managed locking; its absence does not rule out a SQL Server/PostgreSQL deadlock, and the selected victim is not the whole cause.
dbms-deadlock.profile: locks with dbmslocks captures 1C-side participants; obtain the DBMS deadlock report in addition to this profile.

dynamic-list.meaning: A dynamic list opens or scrolls slowly under its real filters, sort order and access rights.
dynamic-list.evidence: Repeated slow SQL during list opening/scrolling and Context leading to that list establish the candidate. [unverified] The exact list-specific cause still needs source-query, filter and rights inspection.
dynamic-list.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for the slow list SQL. 2. Use mode=chain to identify the list call. 3. Reproduce with the problem user's filters, sorting and roles and inspect the plan.
dynamic-list.fixes: Optimize the actual list query, selective predicates and suitable indexes; remove unnecessary fetched data or repeated server access where shown by evidence.
dynamic-list.traps: A fast administrator run does not validate the affected user's access restrictions and data; avoid changing list behavior from one SQL fingerprint alone.
dynamic-list.profile: scenario records opening/scrolling calls and their SQL; db narrows to a persistent expensive list statement after localization.

large-report-result.meaning: A report processes or materializes more data than its output needs, increasing memory and elapsed time.
large-report-result.evidence: CALL MemoryPeak and SQL/result volumes in the report's Context support the candidate; inspect the data composition schema/settings and required output. A peak alone does not prove a leak or an unnecessary result.
large-report-result.investigate: 1. Read report CALL and SQL with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain to relate the query batch and materialization. 3. Compare data composition filters, grouping and actual output size.
large-report-result.fixes: Push valid report restrictions into the query/data composition settings, reduce unnecessary intermediate rows and verify totals and business output after the change.
large-report-result.traps: The IT Expertise example is one ERP report investigation, not a universal memory threshold; compare equivalent settings and data volumes.
large-report-result.profile: scenario captures one report with SQL and CALL counters; memory adds retention diagnostics only when growth persists after report completion.

session-data-growth.meaning: Session-data storage expands or its cleanup/compaction holds the store long enough to affect users.
session-data-growth.evidence: SDGC UsedSize/FilesSize over time for the same InstanceID and LockDuration establish growth/maintenance timing; correlate pauses. Large FilesSize alone does not locate the writer.
session-data-growth.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for related CALL groups. 2. Use mode=events with event=SDGC, then mode=chain on its occurrenceId to inspect nearby work; SDGC has no automatic summary group. 3. Temporarily collect sessiondatacontext to locate changes.
session-data-growth.fixes: Reduce unnecessary session-data changes identified by the diagnostic context; compare UsedSize and compaction lock time after an equivalent workload.
session-data-growth.traps: LockDuration uses milliseconds. SDGC is session storage maintenance, not a BSL heap-leak detector; sessiondatacontext adds overhead.
session-data-growth.profile: No bundled profile includes SDGC by default: add event SDGC to scenario; sessiondatacontext is a separate explicit diagnostic configuration.

exchange-table-writes.meaning: Mass changes and exchange change registration produce heavy writes or DBMS contention.
exchange-table-writes.evidence: SQL and Context must identify exchange change tables and matching DBMS blockers; confirm the registration path. A slow write alone does not establish that exchange registration caused it.
exchange-table-writes.investigate: 1. Inspect write SQL/Context with get_tech_log mode=details. 2. Use mode=chain for transaction and DBMS participants. 3. Check change-table batches and the application's registration logic.
exchange-table-writes.fixes: Review modification batching and exchange registration frequency, shorten demonstrated blocking transactions and validate exchange integrity and delivery after the change.
exchange-table-writes.traps: Borisenko and Grimuta's case is workload-specific; suppressing change registration can damage exchange correctness and is not a generic optimization.
exchange-table-writes.profile: locks with dbmslocks collects write/blocking evidence; lower filtering in db if frequent short registration writes are also relevant.

unexplained-gap.meaning: The full user operation is longer than the work explained by captured event intervals.
unexplained-gap.evidence: A measured action interval and shorter CALL/SQL/lock intervals establish missing explanation, not idle CPU. Check filtered, unfinished and uncollected work before attributing the gap.
unexplained-gap.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details for enclosing call times. 2. Use mode=chain to inspect coverage and child intervals. 3. Expand client/server capture and instrument the code or external operation spanning the gap.
unexplained-gap.fixes: Optimize the demonstrated code, form serialization or external wait after profiling; add focused timing around code not explained by TJ.
unexplained-gap.traps: [unverified] Subtract the union of overlapping child intervals, not their sum; unexplained time is not proven BSL CPU or proof the server was idle.
unexplained-gap.profile: scenario with no duration cutoff preserves short events; include client logs and verify all nodes before diagnosing an unrecorded interval.

bottleneck-moved.meaning: After one constraint is removed, another component limits the operation's response time.
bottleneck-moved.evidence: Comparable before/after whole-operation measurements and changed CALL/SQL/wait/resource distribution support the shift. A later slow run with different data or concurrency is insufficient.
bottleneck-moved.investigate: 1. Use get_tech_log mode=details on comparable pre/post groups. 2. Use mode=chain for representative calls in both captures. 3. Recompare SQL share, waits, memory and client timing under equal conditions.
bottleneck-moved.fixes: Re-run diagnosis and optimize the newly demonstrated constraint; retain the earlier correctness checks and repeat the same full user operation.
bottleneck-moved.traps: Badanov's hardware case illustrates a possible shift, not a guarantee that every optimization exposes another defect; account for changed workload.
bottleneck-moved.profile: scenario is the common comparison capture; add locks or memory instrumentation only when the new distribution indicates that resource.

generation.note: Event/property filters only reduce output. MEM needs mem; LEAKS needs leaks and checkpoints; plans need plansql; DBMS lock annotations need dbmslocks.

plans-disagreement.note: [doc] PostgreSQL methodology restricts plansql to test/development servers. [article: Dmitry Yukhtimovsky] and [article: Nikolay Kuznetsov] older profiles collect plans with slow SQL. Preserve both recommendations and dates (2017 / 2024-2026); do not call plans cheap permanent monitoring.

units-disagreement.note: [article: badcasedaily / OTUS] uses Dur; not documented as equivalent to duration/durationus. [article: Konstmax13] corrected filter units on 2026-10-23. Generate durationus, never Dur. [doc] Historical 8.1 used ten-thousandths of a second; exact transition remains [unverified].

invalid-examples.note: [article: Nikolay Kuznetsov] includes a leading space in SDBL and system nested under log. Documented token is SDBL; system belongs under config.

disk-not-network.note: CALL InBytes/OutBytes are disk I/O despite contrary article interpretations. VRS Body is the request/response body size in bytes, not the body text.

absence.note: Absent does not mean healthy: disabled event, duration filtering, generation settings, missing node, active unfinished call and version can all explain absence.

identities.note: [unverified] Correlation must scope node, process, infobase and interval. Equal numbers across SessionID, t:connectID, ClientID and dbpid do not link identities.

nested-time.note: [unverified] Use union of child intervals for residual time; summing nested durations double counts. Residual time is unexplained by captured events, not proven BSL CPU.

ibsrv.note: [article: Autumn Library] observed file-mode code without CALL and ibsrv CALL depth 0 without t:clientID on macOS 8.3.27. Generality on Windows/Linux and other releases is [unverified]. Never assume only rphost directories.

file-lock-matrix.note: [unverified] No sufficient basis for asserting TLOCK/TTIMEOUT/TDEADLOCK never occur in every file, web and ibsrv mode. Verify each mode/version.

cost.note: No universal MB/day, negligible-overhead, memory, row or process-count thresholds are established. Filters reduce recorded volume, not necessarily instrumentation cost. More than 20 log elements is discouraged.

retention.note: history is hours; 0 disables automatic deletion, not logging. rotationsize is MB per file, not a total directory cap. Gilev short 2-hour, IBS week and analytic long-retention advice serve different tasks.

versions.note: JSON/placement/new rotation arrived in 8.3.25. CALL memory/I/O expanded in 8.3.5; CpuTime in 8.3.13. 8.5.1 filter-unit confirmation does not prove every property unchanged.

source-access.note: ITS lock and deadlock methodologies were available as indexed excerpts (direct 403); gilev.ru pages via index (redirect loops); Burmistrov via index (429); PGConf PDF text only, XML images not transcribed. Books and 2012 attachments were not read; no claims from their unseen contents.

json-unknowns.note: [unverified] Duplicate keys and malformed property names need real-corpus verification. This parser rejects duplicate case-insensitive keys rather than repairing semantics. Unknown event kinds remain readable.

causality.note: [unverified] Keep fact, diagnostic hypothesis, missing evidence and recommendation separate. lka/lkp proves observed blocking, not a deadlock cycle. Carrier event may not be the resource-acquiring SQL.

service-account.note: A service-account cluster does not read the interactive user LOCALAPPDATA. Configuration lookup: version bin/conf, user LOCALAPPDATA/1C/1cv8/conf, ConfLocation, ALLUSERSPROFILE/1C/1cv8/conf. Earlier files shadow later ones.

capture-window.note: Scenario is a short manual bounded reproduction: start, reproduce once, stop immediately; history is retention, not automatic capture expiry.

plans-execution.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes SQL. Do not automatically replay data-changing statements. Reproduce platform connection settings; historic SET lists are not current universal defaults.

instrumentation.note: mem, leaks, scriptcircrefs, query NULL validation and sessiondatacontext add overhead. Full Windows dumps can be large; history does not delete dumps. Linux/macOS dumps use OS facilities.

methodology-scope.note: [doc] Classify whether the slowdown affects all users, one user, the whole system or one function; reproduce on comparable problem-user data. PostgreSQL methodology uses DB time share around 50 percent as a reason to inspect SQL, not a universal failure boundary. [unverified] Nested interval overlap must be removed before interpreting ratios. Use full-user-operation timing, including form serialization/client work outside the BSL timer.

log.meaning: JSON/plain dedicated location, retention hours and size rotation MB.
log.reason: Separate capture ownership and JSON parser compatibility.
log.cost: Size rotation does not cap total disk usage.

event.meaning: OR between event branches, AND between predicates in a branch.
event.reason: Collect selected profile events; filters only reduce generated data.
event.cost: Volume depends on event frequency; no fixed overhead guarantee.

property.meaning: all retains available context and correlation properties.
property.reason: Preserve evidence for details and chains.
property.cost: Larger records; diagnostic values can be sensitive.

durationus.reason: Reduce recorded long-call/DB volume; keep errors and locks unfiltered.
durationus.cost: Short parents and aggregate cost of short DB calls can be hidden.

infobase.meaning: Exact p:processName filter on every branch.
infobase.reason: Restrict a server capture to the requested infobase.
infobase.cost: Excludes client/file events lacking that property.

plansql.cost: [doc] PostgreSQL methodology: test/development only. Older articles differ; plan generation can be expensive even with output filters.

dbmslocks.cost: Extra DBMS queries no more often than once every 2 seconds on DB access; not a complete deadlock graph.

mem.reason: Memory profile or requested MEM event.

leaks.meaning: Track retained objects at server point checkpoints.
leaks.reason: Memory profile or requested LEAKS event.
leaks.cost: Adds overhead; narrow to a procedure after localization.

scriptcircrefs.cost: Substantial performance loss; focused diagnostics only.
